sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Video diffusion transformers (DiTs) generate realistic videos, but their heavy computational cost limits broader real-world applications. Mixed-resolution generation reduces this cost by generating the visually important region at high resolution (HR) and the rest at low resolution (LR), yet existing methods suffer a severe quality drop on videos and require knowing the HR region in advance. We show that these failures are not inherent to mixed resolution, and propose $\textbf{MPEG-Diffusion}$ to address their three root causes: (1) dual-resolution attention to mitigate the curse of mixed resolution, where each query reads the K/V of its own resolution, (2) a mixed-resolution decoder to blend the HR and LR latents before decoding and resolve distortion, and (3) a self-selected HR region using the DiT's knowledge to find the visually important region without requiring it in advance. Processing only $30\%$ of full-resolution tokens, MPEG-Diffusion speeds up denoising by $4.8\times$ on Wan2.1 14B ($3.8\times$ on 1.3B), outperforming prior methods on nearly every metric. In the user study, we demonstrate the high quality of MPEG-Diffusion, with raters preferring it over prior mixed-resolution methods in over $90\%$ of pairs and rating it close to full resolution.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Video diffusion transformers (DiTs) generate realistic videos, but their heavy computational cost limits broader real-world applications. Mixed-resolution generation reduces this cost by generating the visually important region at high resolution (HR) and the rest at low resolution (LR), yet existing methods suffer severe quality drop on videos and require knowing the HR region in advance. We show that these failures are not inherent to mixed resolution, and propose MPEG-Diffusion to address their three root causes: (1) dual-resolution attention to mitigate the curse of mixed resolution, where each query reads the K/V of its own resolution, (2) mixed-resolution decoder to blend the HR and LR latents before decoding and resolve distortion, and (3) self-selected HR region using the DiTs knowledge to find the visually important region without requiring it in advance. Processing only 30% of full-resolution tokens, MPEG-Diffusion speeds up denoising by 4.8 on Wan2.1 14B (3.8 on 1.3B), outperforming prior methods on nearly every metric. In the user study, we demonstrate the high quality of MPEG-Diffusion, with raters preferring it over prior mixed-resolution methods in over 90% of pairs and rating it close to full resolution. 1. Introduction Video diffusion transformers (DiTs) [31] generate videos of striking quality, but attention scales quadratically with the number of tokens as resolution and duration grow, limiting their broader real-world applicability. Yet this compute is spent uniformly: every region of every frame is generated at the same resolution, whether it shows detailed face or plain blue sky. Video coding solved the same problem for transmission decades ago. Codecs such as MPEG and H.264/AVC [32] spend fewer bits on simple or predictable content and more on the regions that matter, which saves large share of the bandwidth at little perceptual cost. We ask whether video Figure 2. Overview of MPEG-Diffusion. The first of steps run at LR. At step k, linear head selects the HR region (part 2), and the remaining steps denoise at HR and the rest at LR. In dual-resolution attention (part 1), each query reads the K/V of its own resolution, with missing entries (dashed) filled from the other resolution by linear maps. The mixed-resolution decoder (part 3) merges the HR and LR latents into one HR video. Flames mark trained parts. generator can do the same with compute. Mixed-resolution generation [4, 18, 36] offers natural mechanism: the visually important region is generated at high resolution (HR) and the rest at low resolution (LR), where one LR token replaces multiple HR tokens  (Fig. 1)  . This cuts the cost of every denoising step in proportion to the LR area. In practice, however, mixed resolution is rarely used for video generation, for two reasons. First, prior mixedresolution methods suffer sharp drop in quality, with blurry details and visible distortion along the resolution boundary. Second, unlike codec that compresses an existing video, generator must know the HR region in advance, when the intermediate frames are still too blurry for an off-the-shelf detector. We argue that these failures are not inherent to mixedresolution generation: we identify three root causes in existing approaches [4, 18, 36] (Sec. 3) and propose MPEGDiffusion  (Fig. 2)  to address each cause: 1. Curse of mixed resolution Dual-resolution attention. When HR and LR tokens share one set of keys and values (K/V), we prove that no single LR token can match the attention of the HR tokens it replaces (Proposition 1), even with fine-tuning. Instead, we propose dual-resolution attention, where linear map fills in the missing K/V from the other resolution (Sec. 3.1), so each query reads the K/V of its own resolution, avoiding the quality drop caused by cross-resolution attention. 2. Resolution mismatch Mixed-resolution decoder. In the VAE decoder, each patch depends strongly on its neighboring patches, so decoding the LR and HR latents separately causes severe distortion at the resolution boundary, even on real videos (Sec. 3.2); hence we propose mixed-resolution decoder to blend them in latent space before decoding. 3. External condition reliance Self-selected HR region. Existing methods require knowing the HR region in advance [4, 18]. Instead, leveraging the DiTs knowledge of the visually important subject across frames  (Fig. 4)  , we use linear layer on the DiT features to predict the HR mask during denoising at negligible cost, enabling plain text-to-video generation. Processing only 30% of full-resolution tokens, MPEGDiffusion speeds up denoising by 3.8 on Wan2.1 1.3B and 4.8 on 14B at near full-resolution quality, outperforming prior methods on nearly every metric at the same token budget (Tab. 1). In blind user study, raters prefer ours over Phase-Aligned RoPE and Foveated Diffusion (98.8% and 90.1% win rates), with 45.2% win rate against fullresolution generation  (Fig. 9)  . 2. Related work Efficient diffusion. Along the token axis, token merging and pruning remove redundant tokens in the intermediate layers of the transformer [2, 3, 6, 13, 35], and sparse attention skips unimportant querykey pairs in video DiTs [37, 40]. Along the time axis, feature caching reuses intermediate features across denoising steps [14, 17], and distillation and consistency models reduce the number of steps [24, 25, 41]. However, all of these methods still generate every region at the same output resolution. We instead vary resolution across regions, orthogonal to these methods. Mixed-resolution generation. LIPAR [18] reuses temporal tokens that are deemed redundant, whereas we focus on spatial redundancy. Phase-aligned RoPE [36] and foveated diffusion [4] generate different regions at different resolutions, the latter around known gaze point. Concurrently, Level-of-Token Diffusion [19] varies the token size across regions, following layout given in advance. While promis2 ing, on video generation their quality drops severely (Tab. 1) and they require the region in advance; we identify and address the three root causes (Sec. 3). Localization from diffusion features. Diffusion features carry rich semantic and spatial information. They can match and track objects without supervision [16, 27, 42], support segmentation [30, 38, 44], and their cross-attention maps localize the words of the prompt [28]. In video DiTs, attention also matches points across frames [20]. Building on this, we read the visually important HR region directly off the DiT with single linear head (Sec. 4.3). 3. Observations: why mixed resolution fails We make three observations on why mixed resolution fails and how to fix it, each of which motivates one component of our method (Sec. 4). 3.1. Observation 1: the curse of mixed resolution Whether an area is generated at HR or LR is design choice: ideally, it should change only how much detail the area has, and approximately maintain its effects on other regions. However, we show that under softmax attention, one LR token cannot maintain the effects of multiple HR tokens when the two resolutions share one set of keys and values (a shared K/V). The mismatch comes from the number of tokens under softmax, not from the weights, so fine-tuning alone cannot fully resolve it. Consider an arbitrary softmax attention head in transformer layer. Assume that we plan to replace high-resolution tokens with keys k1, . . . , kn and values v1, . . . , vn by low-resolution token with key kc and value vc. Let k1, . . . , km and v1, . . . , vm be the keys and values of the other, unchanged regions. Consider an arbitrary scale). Mixed generation fails because LR queries attend to HR K/V or vice versa, breaking this match. Each query should therefore read K/V at its own resolution, with map filling in its missing positions from the other resolution. Such map is likely to exist because an LR token and the HR tokens of its area represent the same content, differing only in fine detail. strong linear relation. To test whether simple linear map suffices, we encode 50 videos at both HR and LR and run the base Wan2.1 1.3B DiT (without fine-tuning) on each resolution separately to collect the HR and LR K/V at every block. Pairing each LR token with the HR tokens at the corresponding spatial-temporal position, we fit one linear map per block and direction: the down map predicts the LR key (or value) from its corresponding HR keys (or values), and the up map does the reverse. On 50 held-out videos, the fitted maps reach an average cosine similarity of 0.96 and 0.85 for down keys and values, and 0.94 and 0.75 for up keys and values (Fig. 21 in the supplementary), indicating strong linear relation between the two resolutions and making dual-resolution attention feasible (Sec. 4.1). Figure 4. The DiT knows where the subject is. linear head on the DiT features at an early denoising step predicts the HR region (bright), which tracks the subject from frame 0 to 80 while the background stays at LR (dimmed). 3.2. Observation 2: VAE neighbor sensitivity Due to the structural constraint of the VAE decoder, which requires uniform spatial grid, mixed-resolution latent cannot be decoded directly because its HR and LR parts have different dimensions. naive solution (resize-andpaste [4]) fills each latents missing region with the resized other latent, decodes them separately, and pastes them together. However, we find that the VAE decoder relies heavily on surrounding patches, so misaligned neighbor corrupts the decoded patch even when the patch itself is correct. To verify this without denoising error, we encode real video at both HR and LR: resize-and-paste still leaves seam along the boundary (Fig. 3a), and filling the missing region with noise spreads the artifacts further (Fig. 3b). This inspires our mixed-resolution decoder (Sec. 4.2), which merges the HR and LR latents into single unified latent before decoding so every patch sees consistent neighbors. 3.3. Observation 3: the DiT knows the important region major challenge of mixed resolution is knowing which region should be HR in advance. MPEG compresses video that already exists, so its motion vectors are known in advance. generator, however, must choose its HR region before the video exists, and early in denoising the predicted video is still too blurry for detector to be reliable. Surprisingly, we find that the DiT itself already knows which region is visually important. single linear layer on the DiT features captures the main subject, even as it moves  (Fig. 4)  . This matches prior work showing that diffusion features can track objects [20, 27]. This property lets us read the HR region directly off the model without knowing it in advance, extending mixed-resolution generation to plain text-to-video (Sec. 4.3). 4. MPEG-Diffusion Based on these observations, MPEG-Diffusion saves compute by generating the visually important regions of video at HR and the rest at LR  (Fig. 2)  . Inference. Generation has four stages: (1) LR generation: the first of steps denoise the whole video at LR; (2) Region selection: at step k, linear head on the DiT features selects the HR region (Sec. 4.3); (3) Mixedresolution generation: we upscale the selected LR region to HR with (by upscaling the clean LR prediction at step and re-noising it), and the remaining steps denoise at HR and the rest at LR with dual-resolution attention (Sec. 4.1); and (4) Decoding: the mixed-resolution decoder merges the two latents into one HR video (Sec. 4.2). Training. We fine-tune the DiT together with the K/V maps and resolution embedding, one learned vector each for HR and LR tokens, added to every token and initialized at zero. Self-selected HR region To enable plain text-to-video generation, we leverage the DiTs ability to locate the visually important region (Sec. 3.3) and read the HR region directly off its features with linear head. Inference. At step k, from the output hb RC of middle DiT block at LR token b, the head scores each token as sb = wLN(hb), (7) where LN is layer normalization and RC is the learned weight. If is below fixed floor, the video has no clear subject and stays fully at LR. Training. We train the head on the frozen DiT and explore two ways to label visually important tokens: (1) self-supervised perceptual label, defined as the per-patch LPIPS [43] between the decoded LR prediction at step and the ground-truth HR video (Sec. G), which directly measures where LR loses detail without external models, but can be distracted by high-frequency background texture; and (2) an object label, where an LLM [22] identifies the main subject from the prompt and Grounded SAM [15, 23] tracks it across frames  (Fig. 7)  . We use the object label at inference, as it better aligns with human attention, and train the head with binary cross-entropy loss. 5. Experiments Setup. We evaluate on both video and image generation. For video, we build on Wan2.1 [31] 1.3B at 480p and 14B at 720p (7041280, so that each LR token covers 22 HR tokens), generating 81-frame videos in 50 steps. The DiT is fully fine-tuned with the K/V maps for 1,250 steps on 64 NVIDIA B200 GPUs; the mixer and upscaler are trained separately for 4k steps, and the region head on about 2,500 labeled clips. For images, we apply our method to FLUX.2 [klein] 4B [1], DiT that, unlike Wan, puts the text and image tokens in one joint attention, at 10241024. Baselines. We compare with token merging (ToMe [2], IDM [35]) and the prior mixed-resolution methods, PhaseAligned RoPE [36] and Foveated Diffusion [4]. Since the gaze region is not available in text-to-video, we follow [4] and run both with circular HR region moving along predefined path at all steps, matching the token count and training data. HR and LR serve as references. Evaluation. We generate one sample per prompt with fixed seed. For video, we report MANIQA [39], imaging quality [10] and DOVER [33] on 1,003 MovieGen [21] prompts and VBench Quality on 944 VBench [8] prompts, together with human study on 400 randomly selected video pairs from MovieGen (Sec. 5.1). For images, we report Q-Align [34] and patch FID [7] on 1,000 held-out prompts, together with GPT-5.6 pairwise test (Sec. I). Speed is the denoising time on one NVIDIA B200, relative to HR. 5.1. Comparison with Acceleration Methods Qualitative. We first compare generated videos with the prior mixed-resolution methods on both Wan2.1 14B and 1.3B. In Fig. 8, both baselines show strong artifacts where the HR and LR regions meet, while our method generates the subject sharply and without seam. This holds across prompts and is even more pronounced when viewed in video; we encourage the reader to view the videos in the supplementary material. Additional visual examples with token layouts are provided in Sec. A. Machine metrics. To quantitatively demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we compare MPEG-Diffusion with token merging and mixed-resolution methods on Wan2.1 1.3B and 14B at the same token ratio. Quality. At both = 40 (a 30% token ratio) and = 25 (38% on 1.3B and 37% on 14B, Tab. 1), our method is the best on every quality metric for both models. The gap is largest on MANIQA, which penalizes local distortions: prior mixedresolution methods leave seams and artifacts around the HR region, and ToMe [2] and IDM [35] collapse into complete noise at this high compression ratio. Our method also comes closest to HR (a DOVER gap of 0.016 on 1.3B and 0.025 on 14B at = 40), preserving near full-resolution quality with only 30% of the tokens needed. While VBench Quality is insensitive to blur (barely separating HR and LR in the 14B case), detail-sensitive metrics (MANIQA, DOVER) and human raters  (Fig. 9)  show clear gap over LR. Speed. On 1.3B, our method is the fastest at = 40 (3.8) and on par at = 25 (2.8). On 14B, it is slightly slower (4.8 vs. 5.2 at = 40), because each HR token attends to the full HR K/V rather than shorter mixedresolution sequence. However, with fewer tokens (30% vs. 37%), our method still beats both baselines in speed (4.8 vs. 4.2) and on every metric. Human evaluation. Metrics do not always match human judgment, so we also run blind pairwise user study on Wan2.1 14B. We compare ours with Phase-Aligned RoPE and Foveated Diffusion, all at 37% token ratio, HR and LR, on 400 uncurated video pairs (100 MovieGen prompts 4 baselines). Each of the 15 raters judges 200 pairs, shown in random order with the two videos in random positions, and picks the one with better visual and temporal quality, or draw. Following Jiang et al. [9], Li et al. [12], we split each draw equally between the two methods. Raters prefer ours over Phase-Aligned RoPE (98.8%), Foveated Diffusion (90.1%) and LR (69.1%)  (Fig. 9)  . Against HR, draw is the most common answer (44%), and HR is only slightly preferred (54.8% vs. 45.2%), though ours is 3.3 faster. Our method outperforms prior mixed-resolution methods and is close to full-resolution quality at fraction of the cost. Study details and win/draw/loss counts are in Sec. E. Higher resolution. To demonstrate the generalizability of MPEG-Diffusion, we also run Wan2.1 14B at 960p with 240p LR track, so each LR token stands for 16 HR tokens (k = 25). Following the same evaluation setting as Tab. 1, we compare our method with Foveated Diffusion [4] at the same token ratio. As shown in Tab. 2, our method stays close to HR (DOVER 0.789 vs. 0.806) at 4.8 the speed and consistently beats Foveated Diffusion on every metric at the same speed, while LR degrades across all quality metrics. Ablation studies Runtime overhead. We profile the runtime of MPEGDiffusion on Wan2.1 1.3B (480p, 81 frames, 50 steps, one GPU, batch size 1) at 30% token ratio, averaging nine runs after one warm-up run. The MPEG components add only 3.0% to the generation time: the K/V maps take 2.4%, the mixer 0.6% and the region head 0.04%, as shown in Fig. 11. Dual-resolution attention. (a) Dual-resolution attention: warping error, 1,003 prompts (b) Mixed-resolution decoder: LPIPS, 100 real clips Figure 13. Error profile across the HR/LR edge (negative distance: HR side; shaded: 95% CI). (a) Dual-resolution attention suppresses the warping-error spike of the shared K/V at the edge (+25% vs. +70%). (b) Our mixer removes the LPIPS spike of resize-and-paste just outside the edge. dual-resolution attention keeps it straight. To quantify this phenomenon, we measure temporal consistency near the edge with temporal LPIPS [5] and the warping error [11]. As the HR region moves, the seam moves with it, so the distortion at the seam changes over time and lowers temporal consistency. At the seam between HR and LR, dual-resolution attention lowers temporal LPIPS from 4.59 to 4.14 102 and the warping error from 2.61 to 1.96 103 (Tab. 5 in the supplementary), indicating less distortion. Figure 13a further confirms this: at the seam, the warping error is much lower with dual-resolution attention, while far from 8 the seam the two models are the same. Mixed-resolution decoder. In Sec. 3.2, we observe that the VAE decoder depends on neighboring patches, so resizing and pasting the two decodes leaves seam. To test whether the mixed-resolution decoder removes this seam, we use 100 real held-out videos. We encode each video at 480p and at 240p, and build mixed latent as in generation: the 480p latent inside random moving circle and the 240p latent outside. We measure the LPIPS of each decoding method on the mixed-resolution latent against the 480p video in pixel space, comparing the mixer with resizeand-paste and LR only. In Fig. 13b, we find that near the HR/LR edge, resizeand-paste shows surge in LPIPS, indicating distortion relative to the 480p video. In contrast, the mixer removes the distortion, lowering LPIPS near the edge from 0.19 to 0.12. Self-selected region. In Sec. 3.3, we observe that DiT features can locate the visually important region. To evaluate our linear head quantitatively, we compare the HR mask it predicts at step against the main-subject mask labeled by the LLM and Grounded SAM (Sec. 4.3) across the 1,003 generated MovieGen videos. The predicted region achieves an mIoU of 0.59 on Wan2.1 1.3B and 0.67 on 14B, showing that the linear head accurately locates and tracks the main subject during denoising. 6. Conclusion We studied why mixed-resolution generation comes with severe drop in quality. We found three root causes and addressed each with one component of MPEG-Diffusion: (1) dual-resolution attention to mitigate the curse of mixed resolution, (2) the mixed-resolution decoder to blend the HR and LR latents before decoding, and (3) linear layer using the DiTs knowledge to find the important region without requiring it in advance. Together, MPEG-Diffusion achieves up to 4.8 speedup, and in our human study raters prefer it over prior mixed-resolution methods in over 90% of the pairs. We hope our work opens the way to mixed-resolution generation. Limitations and future work. Dual-resolution attention assumes linear relation between the HR and LR tokens of an area. This relation is strong in the base model (Sec. 3.1), but it remains structural constraint. This may still lead to slight degradation of the quality. Additionally, the difference between the blurry LR region and the sharp HR details is sometimes obvious, and further work is needed to blend them more smoothly. Finally, the self-selected region is learned from subject labels given by an LLM and Grounded SAM, so we suggest end-to-end fine-tuning as future work.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: LLMs are used in two parts of the method and evaluation, both described in the paper: Qwen2.5 [22] identifies the main subject from the prompt to build the object labels for the region head (Sec. 4.3), and GPT5.6 serves as blind pairwise judge of image quality (Sec. 5.2). We also used an LLM-based assistant to edit the text for grammar and clarity. The authors checked all text and results and take full responsibility for them.
